In addition, the letters were not accompanied by other evidence that would sufficiently corroborate the
Petitioner's claim that the Beneficiary has won nationally or internationally recognized prizes for
excellence in soccer. Wjthout documentary evidence to provide information regarding the actual
competitions themselves, such as the level of those who participated, the selection criteria, or the
degree of attention the events attract within the field, we cannot conclude, based on the name of the
competitions alone, that they are national or international and therefore that the results are recognized
beyond the awarding entities as national or international awards. A competition may be open to
athletes from throughout a particular country or countries, but this factor alone is not adequate to
establish that an award or prize is "nationally or internationally recognized." Further, the Beneficiary's
awards appear to have been received· in age-restricted competition. Even within a national-level
competition, an award given to an athlete competing in age-restricted events would not necessarily be
"nationally recognized." While age restricted awards may be natiqnally or internationally recognized,
the burden is on the Petitioner to demonstrate the level of recognition and achievement associated with
the Beneficiary's awards. Here, it did not demonstrate major trade or general media coverage of the
competitions or equivalent evidence of their recognition in the field, to sho·w that the field nationally or
internat~onally recognizes these as awards for excellence. ·

In order to satisfy this criterion, the petitioner must establish not only that the beneficiary has made
original contributions but that they have been of major significance in the field. For example, it may
support the record with evidence that a beneficiary's contributions have been widely implemented,
have· remarkably impacted or influenced the field, or have otherwise risen to a level of major
significance in the field. Here, while letter states that the Beneficiary's manual has had
an influence on it does not establish the manual's significance to the greater field of
soccer and coaching. Demonstrating ability as a skilled soccer coach is not itself a contribution of
major significance; rather, the Petitioner must demonstrate that the Beneficiary has impacted the field
of soccer or soccer coaching as a whole. C.f. Visinscaia v. Beers, 4 F. Supp. 3d 126, 134-135 (D.D.C.
2013) (upholding a finding that a ballroom dancer had not met this criterion because she did not
demonstrate her impact in the field as a whole). Here, the record does not include documentary evidence
showing the widespread implementation of the Beneficiary's training manual, that it has been seminal,
or that it otherwise equates to an original contribution of major significance in the field.

The Director concluded, without discussion, that the Beneficiary was employed in a critical or essential
capacity as a soccer player "on the Soccer Team," and as a youth soccer coach
for and The scope of this evidentiary criterion focuses on the relative importance of
the Beneficiary's position within the organizations that have employed him. Upon review of the
record, we withdraw the Director's determination.
First, the evidence submitted does not establish that the Beneficiary's participation on 1979
team, and its 1981 team was in a critical or
esse·ntial capacity for the soccer team as a whole. Not every athlete who performs
effectively for a sports team meets this regulatory criterion. The Petitioner did not provide evidence
documenting where the Beneficiary's position fell within the soccer team's general
hierarchy, or evidence that elucidates how his position in Uruguay's youth divisions compared to the top
level soccer athletes on the soccer team. The evidence provided by the Petitioner
does not establish that the Beneficiary was responsible for the soccer team's success
or standing to a degree consistent with the meaning of "critical or essential capacity."
